FOREWORD This Indian Standard (Third Revision) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards, after the draft finalized by the Industrial Gases Sectional Committee had been approved by the Chemical Division Council. The second revision was prepared to upgrade the quality of the gas required by the Electric Lamp Industry by incorporating the limits of impurities, like carbon monoxide, hydrocarbons and oxides of nitrogen etc, which were not described earlier. This high purity hydrogen of 99.9 percent purtiy is also used in the production of butane], octanol, polyurethane, polyamides, aniline and hydrogenation of fats and oils. Since the specification calls for high purity standards, the analysis demand instruments having high sensitivity and precision. Hence, the classical glass test sets, orsat apparatus, etc, have been discarded for high purity gas for which only instrumental methods involving electrochemical analyzer, gas chromatography, etc, have been prescribed. This third revision has been undertaken since it has been now technically possible to produce still higher purity {~radcof 99,999 percent which finds its use in Electronic Industry, necessity has been felt to revise the standard ~ for incorporating the ultra pure grade of the hydrogen gas. Since this grade requires stricter control of impurities, analysis of impurities are done with a different approach. 7'he impurities are concentrated by absorption and determining by chromatography. The composition of the Committee responsible for formulation of this standard is given at Annex N. For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS 2: 1960 `Rules for rounding off numerical values (revised'. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

Collect a sample of the gas freed from carbon dioxide and oxygen in the burette over mercury. Level carefully and note the volume at atmospheric pressure and temperature. Switch on the furnace, adjust the temperature to 350+ 10"C and pass a current of pure nitrogen at the rate of 4 to 5 I/h through the drying tube, copper oxide tube and absorption tube. After sweeping the apparatus with nitrogen to remove any moisture in the copper oxide tube, remove the absorption tube, allow it to cool and weigh. Replace the absorption tube in proper position and, by raising the levelling bottle, introduce the sampIe of the gas slowly into the stream of nitrogen running through the apparatus. After the introduction of the sample of the gas, continue the flow of nitrogen for another 15 to 20 rein, and then remove the absorption tube, cool it and weigh,

atmospheric pressure in mm/Hg, and initial volume in ml of the gas (free from carbon dioxide and oxygen).

to the mark on the pipette and close stopcock A. Allow to cool and note the volume of the residue VIin the burette. Put stopcocks A and B in position 1 and switch off the furnace.

ANNEX B

OF OXYGEN B-1.2 Classical Method
B-1.2.O Two methods are described, namely, Method I and Method 2.

DETERMINATION B-1 INSTRUMENTAL B-1.1 General
Three methods have been prescribed, namely, the electrochemical analyzer, the oxygen analyzer and the gas chromatography.

METHOD

B-1.2.1 Method 1
B-1.2.1.1

Principle

B-1. 1.1 Electrochemical

Analyzer

The oxygen in the test gas reacts with the silver cathode in the galvanic cell contained in the apparatus to produce hydroxyl ions which oxidize metallic cadmium to cadmium hydroxide. This generates a current which flows in the external circuit consisting of a galvanometersconnected across the electrodes. The magnitude of the current is a measure of the amount of oxygen in the gas. The procedure to be followed for the determination of oxygen content shall depend on the type of analyzer used. Manufacturers' instructions in this regard shall be followed.
B-1. 1.2 Oxygen Analyzer

A sample of gas is bubbled through an alkaline solution of pyrocatechol in complete absence of oxygen. The colour developed in the solution due to the reaction of pyrocatechol with oxygen ;n the sample gas is matched with standard colour discs.
B-1 .2.1.2 Apparatus

a)

The assembly of apparatus shall be as shown in Fig. 3, and b) Standard colour discs -- available from the supplters of scientific instruments.

B-1.2.1.3 Reagents
Pyracatechol solution -- Bubble oxygen-free nitrogen from a tested certified cylinder through 1000 ml of distilled water, for half an hour, contained in the bottle D. Divide the distilled water into two portions, one of 900 ml in bottle D, and the other of 100 ml in a small conical flask. Keep both portions bubbling with oxygen-free nitrogen to the 900 ml of water in bottle D, add 7 g of pyrocatechol, maintaining the nitrogen bubbling. To the 100 ml of water in the conical flask, add 6 g of ferrous ammonium sulphate, 1 g of the zinc and 2 ml of concentrated sulphuric acid, still maintaining the nitrogen bubbling and warm the solution gently so that a brisk evolution of hydrogen occurs. When most of the zinc has dissolved, add the solution quickly to the solution in bottle D, transferring the remaining zinc as well. Attach bottle D quickly through the coupling M to the set where this solution as well as that in bottle E is kept bubbling with oxygen-free nitrogen continuously to prevent the entry of atmospheric oxygen. After leaving the reagents, the nitrogen will escape through K atmospheric pressure. b) Sodium @droxide solution -- Take 500 mI of distilled water in a beaker and bubble, fairly vigorously, oxygen-fkee nitrogen through it. Add 250 g of sodium hydroxide in smal I portions to the water while nitrogen is

a)

Oxygen analyzer based on zirconium oxide sensing element measures oxygen concentration in nearly all non-combustible gases and gas mixtures in all proportions. It combines the advance of microprocessor technology with trusted cell design. This uses a stabi Iized zirconium oxide tube, which when hot acts as oxygen concentration cell providing an emf proportional to the oxygen according to the Nemst equation. The procedure to be followed for the determination of oxygen content shall depend on the type of analyzer used. Manufacturer's instructions in this regard shall be followed.
B-1. 1.3 Gas Chromatography

Gas chromatography is a process of separation achieved by means of a partition between a stationary phase and a moving phase. A iuitable synthetic zeolite and suitable detector are used in the gas chromatography. It should be capable to analyzing various impurities up to 1 VPM (ppm by volume).
B-1. 1.3.1 Procedure

Calibrate the instrument against calibration gas of known composition by measuring the peaks or the areas under various peaks of the chromatogram following the instructions of the manufacturer. Carry out the test according to manufacturer's instructions and compute the concentration of various impurities by comparing the peaks or the areas under peaks with that of calibration gas. 5

Turn taps Q and N off so that liquid does not rise into C. Turn K so that nitrogen bubbles through mercury in order to obtain pressure in D and E. Pour water into S with tap R open to the atmosphere until water level isjust below tap R. Half fill bubbler G with water. Fill the bubbler L to height of 62 mm with mercury. Run mercury into reservoir T and raise T until the mercury reaches the fixed mark on F. `I%is height of mercury gives a speed of approximately 15 ml/min. Connect the cylinder or gas supply to be tested to A by means of a flow adjustment valve and glass or copper tubing, any connections being made with rubber pressure tubing and as short as possible. Turn B so that the gas from the cylinder will pass to the atmosphere and carefully open the cylinder valve and flow adjustment valves. When the connections have been thoroughly blown out with gas, reduce the rate of flow to about 2.5 l/h and turn B so that the gas passes into C through the sintered disc. Open the tap

P and allow the gas to pass to the atmosphere through tap R. There should always be a slight excess of gas bubbling through the mercury in F. Allow the gas to pass until C is thoroughly washed out. By turning taps N and Q, force sodium hydroxide solution into C to the 1 ml mark. Turn the tap N to connect C to the pyrocatechol reservoir and force the solution into C to the 10 ml mark. Shut taps Q and N. If the solution in C is only slightly coloured, it is ready for test, but if there is appreciable colour, run it carefully to waste bottle Jby closing tap P, and opening tap Q to waste. Refill C to the 10 ml mark as indicated above. If the solution is still appreciably coloured, the process shall be repeated until an almost colorless solution is obtained.

Match the colour of the solution in C as quickly as possible with a suitable standard on the colour disc using the matching plate and turn tap R immediately so that the gas passes into the measuring burette H. When 100 or 200 ml of gas have passed in, rematch C against suitable standard. If the gas contains appreciable quantity of oxygen, it may only be necessary to use 100 ml of gas to obtain a suitable colour change. 6

METHODS

D-I.O General Three methods have been prescribed, namely electrolytic hygrometers, frost or dew point hygrometer and capacitance hygrometer.
D-1. 1 Electrolytic Hygrometer
is based on the absorption and

dew or frost is formed from the moisture content of the gas at a particular pressure which maybe observed optically in the apparatus. The temperature at which the dew or frost is formed is a measure of moisure content of the gas. The procedure to be followed for determining the moisture content shall depend upon the type of the apparatus to be used. The manufacturer's instructions in this regard shall be followed. D-1.3 Capacitance
Hygrometer

The

instrument

electrolysis

of the water

vapour

present

in the sample

gas. The electrolysis current gives a direct measurement of water vapour present in the gas flowing through the instrument at a steady rate. The procedure to be followed for determining the moisture content shall depend on the type of apparatus to be used. The manufacturer's instructions in this regard shall be followed. D-1.2 Frost or Dew Point Hygrometer A metal surface on the hygrometer is cooled so that 9

The instrument is based on the change of capacitance of the sensor when a sample gas containing water vapour passes through it. The change in capacitance gives a direct measurement of water vapour present in the gas. The procedure to be followed for determining the moisture content shall depend upon the type of the apparatus to be used. The manufacturer's instructions in this regard shal I be followed.

E-1 INSTRUMENTAL
E-1. 1 General

METHOD

E-2.3.2 Phenolphthalein

Dissolve 0.50 g of phenolphthalein rectified spirit. E-2.3.3 Barium Hydroxide Solution

in 100 ml of

Three methods have been prescribed, namely, infrared analyzer, electrochemical method and the gas chromatography method. E-1. 1.1 Infra-Red Analper lnfra-red analyzers are used for determining impurities of hetroatomic gases. The hetroatomic gases absorb energy at characteristic wavelengths when subjected to infra-red radiation. The procedure to be followed for determining the impurities contents shall depend on the type of apparatus to be used. The manufacturer's instructions in this regard shall be followed. E-1. 1.2 Electrochemical
Method

Dissolve about 4 g of barium hydroxide in 2000 ml of water in large flask. Close the flask and shake until the crystals have completely disappeared and a light insoluble powder remains. Allow the solution to stand for two days or until the barium carbonate has completely settled; siphon it into a bottle through which current air (free from carbon dioxide) has been passed for 2 h previously. Assemble this bottle with a soda-lime tube and a burette.
E-2.4 Procedure

When a gas containing carbon dioxide is passed through a reactivated liquid, the electrical conductivity of the liquid changes depending upon the carbon dioxide content. The measurement of the change in electrical conductivity gives a direct measurement of carbon dioxide. The procedures to be followed for determining carbon dioxide shall depend upon the type of apparatus to be used. The manufacturer's instructions in this regard shall be followed. E-1. 1.3 Gas Chromatography The procedure under B-1.1.3. shall be the same as prescribed

Take 25 ml of barium hydroxide solution in each absorber, R, and R, and add carbon dioxide-free water to about half thei~ height. Pass the gas through the spiral absorbers at the rate of about 5 I/h. Measure the rate of flow of the gas by suitable flowmeter and record the temperature and atmospheric pressure at regular intervals. Pass 30 I of gas keeping temperature and pressure of the gas constant. Titrate individual Iy the baryta solution in both the absorbers with standard hydrochloric acid using phenolphthalein indicator and find out the total volume of standard hydrochloric acid used in the two titrations. E-2.4. 1 Carry out a blank titration with an equal volume of barium hydroxide solution used in the two absorbers. G-2 CLASSICAL METHOD G-2.1 Principle Mercury is absorbed in acidified potassium permanganate solution and the excess permanganate is reduced with hydroxyammonium chloride. Mercury is extracted from the solution with dithizone and determined absorptiometrically.

ANNEX H [Table 1, SINO. (viii)]
DETERMINATION H-1 METHODS H-1.O General OF HYDROCARBONS H-1.2 Infra-Red Analyzer

The procedure for determination shall be the same as prescribed in E-1.l.l. H-1.3 Total Hydrocarbon
Analyzer

Three methods have been prescribed, namely, the gas chromatography method, infra-red analyzer and total hydrocarbon analyzer.
H-1.l Gas Chromatography Method

The procedure for determination shall be the same as prescribed in B-1.1.3. 15

The sample gas containing hydrocarbon impurities is burnt in a jet of hydrocarbon in the flame ionization detector and the organic components present in the sample gas provide the source of ions. Concentration of ions is proportional to the concentration of the

Is 1090:2002

organic components. Electrodes having considerably potential difference between them are used to measure the current produced due to ionization and the instrument is calibrated in terms of concentration of hydrocarbons.

H-1.3.1 Calibrate the instrument against calibration gas of known concentration of hydrocarbon following the instructions of the manufacturer. Then carry out the test according to the manufacturer's instructions.

ANNEX J [Table 2, S1 No. (ii), (iii), (v), (vi) and(x)]
METHOD FOR THE DETERMINATION OF OXYGEN, MONOXIDE AND NITROGEN IN HYDROGEN J-1 INTRODUCTION ARGON, CARBON DIOXJDE, CARBON BY GAS CHROMATOGRAPHY Packing Material grade, 250 pm to

J-3.2 Adsorption

This method is suitable for the determination of oxygen, argon, carbon monoxide and nitrogen in electrolytic compressed hydrogen in the concentration range 1 ml to 1000 ml per cubic meter of hydrogen. J-2 PRINCIPLE The impurities in the hydrogen are concentrated by adsorption on silica gel cooled by liquid nitrogen. The silica gel is warmed to room temperature, the impurities desorbed and determined by gas chromatographyy. The gas chromatography is fitted with two packed columns and uses katharometer detection. The hydrogen complies with the specification with respect to oxygen content if the combined argon and oxygen contents are lower than 10 ml/m3 (10 ppm) but, if they exceed this figure, a further determination should be carried out to measure the oxygen content alone. This can be done by the method described in this Annex but using a 9 m molecular sieve 5A column instead of 2.7 m molecular sieve 13 x column. J-3 REAGENTS The following reagents (all of which shall be of analytical reagent quality) are required. J-3. 1 Drying Tube Materials
J-3. 1.1 Phosphorus J-3. 1.2 Asbestos Pentoxide

Silica gel, gas chromatographic 500 pm particle size. J-3.3 Column Materials

FORDETERMINATION OF GASEOUSIMPURITIES INH2

which concentrates impurities in the hydrogen. Adsorption tube (1) is used as a hydrogen purification system in which the impurities are removed to provide a pure stream of hydrogen gas for describing the concentrated impurities from adsorption tube (2) and for the calibration of the gas chromatography. The impurities are desorbed from adsorption tube (2) by passing 3 ml x 100 ml portions of purified hydrogen gas through the tube at ambient temperature. Each 100 ml portion of gas is passed into a gas syringe which acts as a reservoir and part of the gas is transferred to a gas chromatographic column in a sampling valve. A phosphorus pentoxide drying tube is provided to remove water from the hydrogen so as to ensure that the silica gel in the adsorption tubes retains its efficiency for adsorbing the impurities from the hydrogen stream.

J-5.4 Analysis
J-5.4.1 Treatment of Sample J-5.4.1.1 Purging apparatus

Close all the valves in the adsorption system, open the sample cylinder valve and adjust the pressure regulator to 70 kPa. Immerse adsorption tube (I) (J-4.1 .4) in liquid nitrogen. Open valves (4) and (6) to allow hydrogen to pass through the gas meter (J-4. 1.8) to atmosphere. Control the purified hydrogen flow at 60 I/h to 70 I/h with valve(1). Purge for 5 min and then reduce the hydrogen flow to 5 I/h with valve (1). Inject a sample of hydrogen on to the required columns to check that the hydrogen is free from impurities. Close valve (6) and open valve (5). Inject via the injection point (J-4.1 .6) a known volume of the pure gas to be detected using the gas syringe (J-4.1 .7) fitted with a hypodermic needle. Air can be used to calibrate oxygen and nitrogen simultaneously. When the 100 ml gas syringe is tilled with hydrogen plus the gas to be detected shut valve (4) and allow 30 s for the gases to mix. Open valve (6) and pass the gas from the syringe into the gas chromatography (J-4.2.1) and sample loop (J-4.2.4) and inject the sample onto the required column (see J-5.4.3 for typical relative retention times). Measure the peak heights of the components, to the nearest millimetre, and multiply by the attenuation setting to give the peak height in millimetres at attenuation x 1. Repeat the injection of the calibration gas at two further levels covering the expected concentrated range in the sample. Calculate the factor F, in millilitres of component equivalent to 1 mm peak height at attenuation x 1, for each component from the following formula:

With all valves shut and the adsorption tubes at ambient temperature, open valves (2), (4) and (6) and control the flow at 60 l/h to 70 l/h with valve (2). Purge for 5 min. Close valves (2) and (4), open valves (1) and (3) and control the flow at 60 I/h to 70 1/11 with valve (1). Purge for 5 min. J-5.4.1.2 Concentration
of impurities

Reduce the flow to 10 l/h with valve (1) and place the Dewar flask (J-4.1.5) containing liquid nitrogen, around adsorption tube (2) (J-4.1.4) with the si 1ica gel (J-3.2) well below the surface of the liquid nitrogen (J-3.6). Note the reading on the volumetric gas meter (J-4.1.8), close valve (l), open valve (2) and adjust the flow to 60 l/h to 70 I/h and pass approximately 200 1 of gas through the adsorption tube. J-5.4.1.3
concentrate Collection and injection of impurity

Place a second Dewar flask containing liquid nitrogen around adsorption tube (1) with the silica gel well below the surface of the liquid nitrogen. Note the reading on the volumetric gas meter, close valves (2) and (3) and open valves (1) and (4). Check that the gas syringe is free from impurities as follows: close valve (6), open valve (5) and fill the syringe to the 100 ml mark, controlling the flow with valve (1). Close valve (1) open valves (5) and (6) and pass the gas from the syringe through the chromatography sample valve and inject onto the chromatography (J-4.2.1). Repeat this syringe check until no air is detected by the chromatography detector, using maximum sensitivity. Close valves (4) and (6), open valves (3) and (5), remove the liquid nitrogen from around adsorption tube (2) and allow to warm to ambient temperature. Open valve (1) and fill the syringe to the 100 ml mark, close valve (1) and allow 30s for the gas in the syringe to mix. Open valve (6) and pass the gas from the syringe into the sample valve of the chromatography and inject on to the appropriate column of the chromatography.Fill the syringe twice more and inject onto the chromatography,to give three chromatograms for the samples. K-1 PRINCIPLE The mercury vapour is removed from the hydrogen by scrubbing with potassium permanganate/sulphuric acid mixture. After the addition of the hydroxylamine in acid solution to decolonize the permanganate and bring in to the solution any precipitated manganese dioxide, an aliquot portion is taken for mercury determination by flameless atomic absorption method. K-4.2 Preparation of Sample Solution

Set up the instrument as in the calibration procedure (K-4.1). Into the aeration flask pipette 20.0 ml of the sample solution, dilute to 60 ml with water and mix. Add 2.0 ml of the tin (II) chloride solution (K-2.4) and immediately reassemble the apparatus. Operate the 4-way tap and record the instrument response. Carry out a blank on the reagents using 16.0 ml of the absorbing solution (K-2.8) developed by the addition, drop by drop, of the hydroxylammonium chloride solution (K-2.3). Read off the mercury contents of the sample solution and blank from the solution graph. If an off-scale reading is obtained with 20 ml of sample solution, repeat the determination using a smaller aliquot portion. K-5 EXPRESSION OF RESULTS Mercury content, in milligrams per cubic metre of hydrogen, is given by the following formuIa:
(M, -M2)x~ q

Set up the absorption train as shown in Fig. 10. Into each of the Drechsel bottles (K-3.1.2), place 40 ml of the potassium permanganate/sulphuric acid mixture (K-2.8) and attach to the hydrogen sample supply. Allow hydrogen to pass through the absorption train at a rate of about 20 I/h until a suitable sample volume has been passed; about 201 to 401. Disconnect the Drechsel bottles and add the hydroxylammonium chloride solution (K-2.3) until the permanganate colour is just discharged. Swirl, replace the gas distributors, and allow to stand to dissolve any deposits of manganese dioxide. Transfer the contents of both bottles to a 100 ml onemark volumetric flask using a minimum of wash water, dilute to mark and mix.

L-2.3.3 Calibration

Hydrogen is passed at a constant rate through a tube containing calcium carbide where the water reacts to form acetylene. 2 HZO+ CaCz = Ca (OJ-1)2 + Cz H2 The concenb-ation of acetylene in the hydrogen is then determined by gas chromatography using a Porapak T column and flame ionization detector. L-2 REAGENTS L-2.1 Calcium carbide, particle size 150 pm to 200 pm, essentially free from calcium oxide or hydroxide. Carbide granules should be crushed, in small quantities, and sieved in a dry atmosphere and care should be taken to minimize contact with moisture. Store in a glass container sealed with a rubber bung, having a 6 mm hole drilled through it, which is sealed with a short length of glass or steel rod. L-2.2 Column Packing
Porapak T 150 pm to 200 pm particle size.

Acetylene minimum purity 95 percent. L-2.4 Molecular Sieve 5 A 3 mm pellets activated before use by heating at 400�C in a stream of dry nitrogen for 16 h. L-4 PROCEDURE L-4.1 Preparation of Apparatus

L-4. 1.1 Chromatography Column Pack with the Porapak T (L-2.2) and condition by heating to 180 `C for 16 h with the carrier gas (L-2.3.1) flowing through it at 60 ml/min. lrtstall the column (L-3.5.4) in the gas chromatography (L-3.5) and further condition by purging for 16 h with nitrogen at an oven temperature of 100"C, using a flow rate of 60 ml/min and with the column outlet disconnected from the detector (L-3.5.5). L-4. 1.2 Calcium Carbide Reactor (see Fig. 11) Plug one end of the stainless steel tube (L-3.2.1) with a small piece of the superfine glass wool (L-3.2.5). Fit a 6 mm to 3 mm reducing coupling (L-3.2.3) to this end. Remove the plug from the bung of the calciuln carbide (L-2.1 ) container and insert the open end of the stainless steel tube (L-3.2.2) into the hole of the bung. Invert the container and tap the tube gently to start the calcium carbide flowing into the tube. Continue tapping until the tubes are fill. With the reactor in a horizontal position, carefully ease it away from the container, avoiding spilling any of the calcium carbide from the tube or the container, then replace the plug in the calcium carbide container bung. Remove calcium carbide from the end of the reactor tube to a depth of 5 mm and plug the end with superfine glass wool (L-3.2.5). Fit a 6 mm to 3 mm coupling. [f the reactor is not to be used immediately, both ends should be sealed with the 3 mm stainless steel rod (L-3.2.4).

for 5 min. Withdraw 50 ml of the calibration mixture via the bottom septum and inject on to the chromatography(L-3.5.1 ) via the gas sampling valve. L-4.4 Analysis Connect the stainless steel diaphragm pressure regulator (L-3.1) to a well purged sample point and purge to atmosphere at about 1 l/rein for a minimum

The water content expressed as millilitres of water vapour (HZO) per cubic litre of hydrogen is equal to twice the acetylene content determined.

of 15 min. Connect the calcium carbide reactor tube (L-3.2.1) to the regulator and adjust the hydrogen flow to within the range 0.5 l/rein to 1.0 Vrnin, using the volumetric gas meter (L-3.3) and a stopwatch and allow to purge for 15 min at constant temperature to establish equilibrium conditions in the tube. Insert the needle of the 100 mm gas syringe (L-3.4.5) through the septum and slowly withdraw 100 ml of gas into the syringe. Purge the syringe twice with the sample. Finally fill the syringe, remove from the septum and purge the gas sample valve and loop with 50 ml of sample. Pause for 1 s to allow the gas pressure in the sample to attain atmospheric pressure and inject on to the column (L-3.5). Adjust the amplifler attenuation (L-3.5.5.1 ) to give, if possible, an acetylene peak of at least one-third full scale. Carry out a blank determination on an unreacted sample of hydrogen at the same amplifier attenuation. Purge the sample valve with nitrogen between determination.
